summary: You produced a working brute-force implementation that passed all visible tests and most hidden tests, but it times out on at least one large hidden case. The main gap was complexity reasoning: you asserted O(n) and “already optimal,” but the submitted approach is O(n^2) and conflicts with the problem’s constraints and the expected hash-map solution.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed; 1 hidden test failed, consistent with performance/time-limit issues from an O(n^2) approach.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Returned correct indices for typical cases and avoided using the same element twice by scanning j from i+1. Covered a fallback return when no pair is found (even though the prompt guarantees exactly one answer).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Align the implementation with the constraints by switching to the O(n) hash-map approach; otherwise the solution is not complete for the required input sizes (as shown by the hidden failure).

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Started with a clear baseline strategy (brute force over pairs) and implemented it cleanly without logical mistakes on small/medium inputs.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Practice recognizing when constraints force a different technique (here: “exactly one answer” + n up to 1e5 strongly signals a single-pass hash map), and proactively pivot once performance requirements are stated.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You described your intended approach succinctly and confirmed visible-test success.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Be precise when explaining complexity: explicitly account for the inner loop as dependent on n; a good habit is to state the summed work (e.g., (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1) rather than describing the inner loop as “part of processing.”

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You correctly noted the brute-force solution uses O(1) extra space.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Revisit Big-O analysis for nested loops and learn the canonical Two Sum optimization: single pass + hash map (seen value -> index) to achieve O(n) time, which is required here.

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Code is straightforward, readable, and avoids off-by-one issues. Early return on finding the answer is clear.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Remove unnecessary guard clauses that contradict problem guarantees (e.g., `if not nums: return []`) or at least explain why you keep them; and structure the solution around a `seen` dict to meet constraints.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You implemented a baseline solution without needing hints and quickly got all visible tests to pass.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Even without hints, independence includes self-correcting based on constraints; work on independently identifying when an approach will not scale (n=1e5 implies you must move beyond O(n^2)).

thinking_and_logic: Your chosen approach was the brute-force baseline: for each index i, scan all later indices j to check whether nums[i] + nums[j] equals target. That logic is correct for finding a valid pair and prevents reusing the same element by enforcing j > i. However, the reasoning broke down in complexity analysis: a nested scan over remaining elements per i results in quadratic total work, which violates the explicit performance requirement for large inputs.
code_assessment: The final code matches the answer key’s brute-force solution (nested loops), which is correct on many cases but has O(n^2) time and is not acceptable under the stated constraints—this is consistent with passing 9/10 tests and failing a hidden performance case. The canonical optimal solution is a single pass with a hash map of seen values to indices: for each num, compute complement = target - num, check if complement is already in the map, and if so return the stored index and current index; otherwise store num -> i. That achieves O(n) time and will pass the largest hidden test that your current approach likely times out on.

next_steps.action: Rewrite Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (seen value -> index) pattern and re-run against large random inputs (e.g., n=100000).
next_steps.why: This is the canonical optimal approach (O(n) time) required by the constraints and is exactly what your current solution is missing.
next_steps.how: Implement: `seen = {}`; loop i, x; `c = target - x`; if c in seen: return [seen[c], i]; else seen[x] = i. Then benchmark vs your nested loops on increasing n to internalize the scaling difference.

next_steps.action: Drill complexity analysis for nested loops by writing the total-operations sum explicitly.
next_steps.why: You misclassified an O(n^2) double loop as O(n); this will repeatedly cause incorrect solution selection in interviews.
next_steps.how: For this code, write: inner iterations = (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1 = n(n-1)/2 => O(n^2). Do this exercise for a few patterns: full nested loops, triangular loops, and two pointers.

next_steps.action: Practice the common Two Sum variants: sorted array (two pointers) and returning values vs indices.
next_steps.why: Interviewers often follow up; knowing when to use hash map vs two pointers demonstrates pattern fluency.
next_steps.how: Solve: (1) sorted input => left/right pointers O(n) time O(1) space; (2) unsorted input => hash map O(n) time O(n) space; (3) handle duplicates carefully.

encouragement: Your baseline implementation is clean and logically correct; once you pair that with accurate complexity analysis and the hash-map optimization, this becomes a solid, interview-ready solution.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
